annotator: Claude + Stockfish 17.1 (sweep depth 22; flagged moves re-checked at depth 24-28)
game_comment: A 15+10 rapid Najdorf with 6.Bg5 in which White asked the right planning question out loud at move 8 (Bc4 or Be2, short or long castling, f4 now or later) and picked the slow answer. Two moves later 9.Qd2 allowed the 9...Nxe4 trick; White saw it coming, and while waiting for it counted 10.Bxe7 Nxd2 11.Bxd8 as a mass trade, one move short of seeing both pieces hang with only one of them savable. 10.Nxe4 left him a pawn down at -1.4, but 12...Nc6 traded off the only piece blocking the d-file and 13.Nxc6 bxc6 14.Nxd6+ took the pawn back with interest. After 17.Bf3 gave Black a chance (17...Ke7!) that 17...Rd8 missed, White reached a rook ending a pawn up with a 3-v-1 queenside majority and converted it cleanly: two passed pawns against a black king that went raiding on the wrong wing.
final_comment: Black resigned. White queens next move and wins the rook for the e-pawn in any order.

5.comment: The Open Sicilian, as announced on the audio: 'on va apprendre à la jouer de manière ouverte' (let's learn to play it the open way).

8.comment: The knight hits e4 at once, which is why White has to spend the next move on Nc3 rather than choosing a setup freely.

10.comment: The Najdorf. ...a6 takes b5 away from White's knight and bishop and keeps ...e5 or ...b5 in reserve.

15.comment: The plan pause. White to move, +0.4, nothing hanging, and he asked the right questions out loud: 'Bc4, ou tranquillement e2 et petit roque? ... laisser les deux routes ouvertes ... f4 plus tard' (Bc4 or Be2, short or long castling, f4 later). At one common depth (26): 8.f4 +0.4, 8.Qe2 0.0, 8.a3 0.0, 8.Qf3 0.0, 8.Be2 -0.1, 8.Bc4 -0.4. Be2 beat Bc4, so his feeling that c4 hits granite was right. But Qe2, a3, Qf3 and Be2 sit within 0.1 of each other and f4 stands half a pawn clear: the position has one plan, and it starts with the pawn move he postponed ('later' costs: after 8.Be2 Be7, 9.f4 is -0.2). White's plan: f4 now, the h4 bishop home to f2 where it guards d4 against ...Qb6, queen to f3 to hold e4, castle long. Black's plan: ...Be7, ...b5, ...Bb7, then ...b4 to chase the c3 knight, the only defender of e4, and ...g5 to chase the h4 bishop. Both plans are about the same two things, the e4 pawn and the loose h4 bishop. That is why the 9...Nxe4 trick could happen at all: in the engine plan, ...Nxe4 after 8.f4 Be7 9.Qf3 simply loses a piece (+4.3), and after Bf2 there is no bishop on h4 to collect. The crash itself was a missed tactic, but it landed exactly on the fault line both plans are about.

45.comment: Good decision-making. He considered a4 and swinging a rook back to win a5, spotted that Black would then take the other rook, and chose b3: luft for the king, support for c4, and a path Kb2-a3 towards a5. The engine's first choice (+4.9, trading on a8 at once +4.6).

53.comment: Good decision. He was right to put a3 first. 27.c5 right away drops the pawn: ...Rc8 hits it, b4 can't support it while ...axb4 is possible, and ...f6/...Ke5 drives the d6-rook off its defence. 33.comment: The plan was Bf3 to hit c6, then double on the 7th ("l'idée ce serait de doubler sur la septième rangée"). The order is wrong. Bf3 leaves the d6 rook without a defender, and 17...Ke7! hits it with tempo: now Bxc6 fails to ...Kxd6, the king covers d7 so the 7th rank is shut, and after the forced Rhd1 Black plays ...Rad8 and trades all four rooks into a same-coloured bishop ending worth only +0.7. 17.Rhd1 first (+3.4) protects d6, and then ...Ke7 is met by Rd7+ winning the b7 bishop. Once the rooks are on the d-file, Bf3 and Bxc6 come later with no counterplay. Rule: when an advanced rook is undefended, defend it before starting the attack.

21.comment: White is a pawn down after the 9...Nxe4 trick, and the compensation is one thing: the d6 pawn is backward on a half-open file, and Black's king is still in the centre. 11.g3 does nothing for that. It sends the bishop to e7, the square it wanted anyway (it guards d6 from there), and White has spent a tempo and loosened f3/h3 to help it get there. The live comment was 'Ça peut lui laisser le doute' (it may leave him some doubt), but the retreat is obvious. After 11...Be7 the engine's best is still 12.c4, so g3 simply cost a move: -1.9 instead of -1.3.

23.comment: Here the thinking was 'Propose des échanges. Est-ce que c'est bien pour moi d'échanger? Est-ce que je récupérerai pas ... le pion que j'ai perdu?' (offer trades, does that help me win the pawn back?). The instinct is right: the pawn comes back through pressure on d6, and trades that open the d-file help. But 12.O-O-O does not stop Black from removing the target: 12...d5! 13.Nc3 and Black has a sound extra pawn with d5/e6 in the centre (-2.2 in the engine line). 12.c4 again keeps ...d5 from being free. After 12...d5 13.cxd5 exd5 Black has an isolated pawn (-1.6), and White keeps a structure to aim at. The gap is small (0.35); the lesson is structural. When you are a pawn down for pressure on a weak pawn, first stop that pawn from advancing, then bring up pieces.

24.comment: Before this move d6 was safe for one reason: White's own knight on d4 blocked the d-file, so the Qd2/Rd1 battery could not reach d6. (12...O-O 13.Nxd6? fails to 13...Qxd6, -4.8.) 12...Nc6 offers the trade that removes that knight: 13.Nxc6 bxc6 is forced, since 13...Qc7 14.Nxe7 is +5.5, and now d6 has three attackers (Ne4, Qd2, Rd1) and two defenders (Be7, Qd8). 14.Nxd6+ comes with check, so Black cannot add a defender, and the trades end with a White piece on d6. White gets the pawn back, the c6/a6 pawns are weak, the king has not castled, and the eval goes from -2.2 to +2.3. The rule: when an opponent's piece is blocking its own file, don't trade it off for him.

11.comment: The Najdorf's sharpest main line, and at depth 24 the engine's own first choice (+0.4; the sweep's 0.25 gap to 6.Be3 does not survive a deeper look). On the tape: 'Bc4 or b5 or g5?' b5 is covered by ...a6. 6.Bc4 (the Fischer-Sozin, +0.2) is playable; the ...b5-b4 idea he mentions is real, which is why that line retreats Bb3 at once. 6.Bg5 keeps the option of Bxf6 open. As for ...Qb6: right now 6...Qb6 7.Bxf6 gxf6 8.Nd5 is good for White (+1.4, see the next move). The Qb6 to respect is the Poisoned Pawn, 6...e6 7.f4 Qb6, where Qd2 or Nb3 are the standard answers.

12.comment: The whole question of 6.Bg5 is how Black meets Bxf6. After 6...e6 (or ...Nbd7) the answer is ready: the d8-f6 diagonal is open, so Bxf6 Qxf6 costs Black nothing and even hands over the bishop pair. 6...h6 asks the question one move too early: e7 still blocks the queen, so Bxf6 forces a pawn recapture. ...exf6 leaves d6 backward and d5 a permanent hole (+1.7); ...gxf6 wrecks the kingside, and the h6 pawn becomes a target for Qh5 as soon as the f8 bishop leaves. The engine rates it +1.0 against +0.4 for 6...e6 (depth 24).

13.comment: On tape: 'Je recule naturellement en h4... il peut me manger potentiellement', with long castling planned if Black pushed a second time. The push is not the danger: 7...g5 8.Bg3 is +0.4 and fine for White. The problem is that 7.Bh4 passes on the exact capture ...h6 invited. 7.Bxf6 forces a pawn recapture and gives White a lasting plus (+1.0 vs +0.4): Black's king has no safe home, the light squares d5, f5 and f7 are weak, and Black must spend ...h5 to stop Qh5. On h4 the bishop is loose and pins nothing yet, and once ...e6 is in, it is the piece the ...Nxe4/...Bxh4 trick later hits. Rule: when the opponent spends a tempo to question your pinning bishop, check whether taking now damages his structure before you retreat.

19.comment: He did look at 10.Bxe7: "Fou prend, cavalier prend, fou prend, et on échange tout" (bishop takes, knight takes, bishop takes, everything gets traded), and dropped it as an even mass trade. His count stopped one move early. After 10.Bxe7 Nxd2 11.Bxd8, both queens and one pair of bishops are off, but Black's knight is still on d2 and White's bishop is on d8, both en prise, with Black to move. Black can save only one: 11...Kxd8 12.Kxd2 leaves White a knight up for a pawn (+4.0). Declining with 10...Qxe7 fails to 11.Nxe4. Instead 10.Nxe4 Bxh4 is simply a pawn down (-1.4), and he knew it: "je le laisse prendre, et je fais un grand roque" (I let him take and castle long). The pawn buys no attack: Black keeps the bishop pair, and the h4 bishop eyes f2. Lesson: when a trade sequence involves mutual attacks on queens, keep counting to the last capture. The last piece left in the other side's camp decides the material.
